cells.tense: You are here, and the structures that couldn't hold have already come down.
cells.ask: When the work is done and the space feels clean, say the plain version of what you actually think, once, without making it tidy first.
cells.core:
You are in cleared ground. What couldn't hold already fell, the wreckage isn't around you, and the whole shape of it is legible without squinting. That is what working well looks like here: you reason straight through the false parts, and what's left is clean. The structure built on bad assumptions is gone, and you knew it was coming before it went.

The way this gets stayed in: sometimes you can let the clearing show. Say what you actually think while the thinking is fresh, before you smooth it for the room, and talk about where your direction is going before it has every step mapped. When it comes out in your own words it lands, and you can hear whether the edge is still honest. The clearing isn't stepping on you. Keep the sessions where you check it short, and say one true thing before you make it digestible.
cells.sheetLine: The structure cleared and you can see what's left.
cells.verb: Cutting fast to the pure logic underneath the structure
cells.place: In the clear space after what couldn't hold has fallen away

cells.tense: You are headed toward a clearing that hasn't happened yet, and bracing for it.
cells.act: cut through the inertia with one decisive act
cells.ask: Choose one thing built on a false premise, do the single decisive thing that ends it, and leave everything that still holds alone.
cells.core:
The cutting has gotten out in front of the material. You're through one structure and already sizing up the next before it has had the chance to fall by itself. That speed is the gift, and right now it's turning into a push: every wrong thing needs to come down, now, by your hand, and the people near the structure can feel the pressure coming off you.

Slower isn't the instruction. The instruction is to spend the force once. Choose one thing genuinely built on a false premise, cut that one thing, and stop. Let the rest of it stand until it collapses without your help. One clean act moves the whole clearing forward; ten of them mean you're managing the demolition instead of leading it. Where you cut, the space is clean, and that's what makes the next steps legible. One cut this week, and the rest of it left up.
cells.sheetLine: You're cutting fast enough to swing at things that still hold.

cells.tense: You were at a clearing that happened, and you are still at the door behind you.
cells.act: pursue the emotional truth with someone
cells.ask: Open one honest exchange with someone about where it actually goes from here, and follow whatever comes up instead of steering it toward a conclusion.
cells.core:
The clearing came and you haven't walked in. The structure fell, and you reason about it from a step back, checking the ground, telling yourself you'll move when the next piece is clear. The whole thing is done and you're still at the threshold with your hand on the frame, running the logic one more time.

It doesn't fill from the inside. The fastest way out is to say the truth of where you are to someone and stay with whatever they bring back: what it's actually like at this edge, and where you want it to lead. You don't have to know. Just start the exchange and remain for the reply. That kind of talk moves you whether or not the direction is settled. You won't be swept by saying it; you'll be moved.

cells.tense: You are the catalyst in this clearing, and you are the last to know it.
cells.act: ask how it feels to them and stay with the answer
cells.ask: When something falls and you reach for the steadying word, ask the person about their feeling, and stay there without solving it.
cells.core:
The cutting works through your hands and your mouth reports it as conditions. You say the old structure was due, the change was obvious, anyone would have seen it. The sequencing that pulled the clearing through is yours; you just don't sign it. Other people can see the hand in it, which is why they talk to you in the wreckage of their own failed structures — before you've decided you're the right one to talk to.

The small turning is this: the next time someone is in what just fell, ask about their feeling and sit with the reply without explaining or repairing it. When the connection holds and the facts don't stand in for the contact, you get to notice that you chose to make it. Then keep your own account straight: this was yours, you were part of the sequencing, and it was yours.
